title.en: Choose texture sampling from screen footprint

summary: Choose source resolution, UV allocation, mip filtering and bounded anisotropy from the texture's projected use across target cameras and drawing-buffer pixels rather than a universal texture-size rule.
objective: Important surfaces receive enough sampled detail for their largest and most oblique intended views while minified views remain stable, without allocating identical resolution to every asset.
applies_when: A UV-mapped texture appears blurry, pixelated, shimmering or wastefully large across known target cameras, display sizes or oblique surface angles.
intent_signals: what texture resolution does this camera need
reduce distant texture shimmer without one huge map
choose anisotropy for an oblique floor texture
example_prompts: Size a hero prop atlas for one close camera and several distant views without forcing 4K on every prop.
Choose mip and anisotropy settings for a tiled floor seen at a grazing angle.
negative_signals: one pixels-per-metre target fits every shot
not_for: Choosing color-space annotations or PBR channel meaning.
A measured memory or frame-time budget without authorized runtime profiling.

principles: Texture need is view dependent. Use the largest projected footprint of the important textured region across target cameras and actual drawing-buffer pixels, then account for UV coverage and intentional reuse; object dimensions alone do not determine resolution.

Magnification filtering cannot reconstruct authored detail absent from the source. Minification needs a declared filter/mipmap policy to reduce aliasing; oblique footprints may benefit from bounded anisotropy when the selected backend and device support it.

Spend resolution by consequence: labels, hero details and close inspection may need more UV area, while distant or noisy surfaces can tolerate less. This is an artistic and product decision constrained by observable views, not a universal aesthetic budget.

Asset sampling and runtime capability share ownership. Blender owns source image choice, UV allocation and padding; glTF carries supported sampler state; Three.js owns loaded filtering, mip availability, anisotropy cap and drawing-buffer/camera regime.
implementation: List target cameras, viewport and pixel-ratio regimes, closest expected distance, oblique angles and which surface details must remain readable. Capture each important UV island's fraction of source-image texels and its projected screen bounds in those views.

Compare available texels along the island's important axes with projected drawing-buffer pixels. Increase source resolution or UV allocation only where magnification exposes missing information; reduce waste where large allocations never approach the screen footprint.

Choose and record glTF/Three.js magnification and minification filters plus mip availability. Test minified motion and distance changes for shimmer or moiré separately from close-view blur; preserve mip-safe island padding in atlases.

For grazing views, raise texture anisotropy only up to the renderer/device-reported support and only when the view benefits. Treat extra samples as a runtime tradeoff to measure later, not a free quality switch or a guarantee of recovered detail.
Retest after camera FOV, viewport pixel ratio, UV transform, atlas packing or texture compression changes, since each can change the effective screen-to-texel footprint.
observable_checks: At the closest required view, declared labels and hero features remain legible without relying on magnification to invent absent source information; nonessential distant detail may remain simplified.
Across the intended distance sweep, mip transitions do not introduce unacceptable shimmer, moiré or seam bleed under the recorded sampler and atlas padding policy.
At the most oblique required view, a bounded anisotropy comparison is reported against the device cap; improvement or no benefit is recorded without turning the setting into a universal mandate.
A camera, pixel-ratio or UV-layout change triggers a footprint reassessment instead of preserving a stale texture-size choice by habit.

creative_affordances: Deliberate pixel art, painterly blur, nearest filtering or coarse distant textures are valid when they serve the intended image and stay stable in motion.
Concentrate atlas area on narrative details and use repetition or procedural variation elsewhere.
known_limits: No universal texture dimension, texels-per-metre, anisotropy value or acceptable blur threshold is asserted.
Compression quality, shader derivatives, backend sampling and display characteristics can create additional limits beyond this rule.
Runtime cost and memory effects require measured artifact evidence; none is claimed here.
Authored source-checked reasoning; no texture, camera, renderer or device comparison was run.

claims.statement: glTF 2.0 sampler state distinguishes magnification and minification filters, includes mipmap minification modes, and recommends runtime mip generation or defined non-mipmap fallback when mip generation is unavailable.
claims.scope: Core glTF 2.0.1 sampler semantics; it does not choose source resolution, atlas padding or a quality threshold.

source_refs.locator: Texture Data > Samplers > Filtering; sampler.magFilter and sampler.minFilter

claims.statement: Three.js Texture documents separate magFilter and minFilter controls, optional mipmap generation, and anisotropy where higher values can reduce oblique-axis blur at the cost of more texture samples; WebGLRenderer exposes the drawing-buffer size in physical pixels and a maximum available anisotropy query.
claims.scope: Live Three.js Texture and WebGLRenderer documentation read 2026-09-08; actual benefit and cost are backend-, device-, texture- and view-dependent.
